02.r: The toll collector already introduced in the parable.

03.r: Turns from the Pharisee's prayer to the toll collector's.
03.n: The Textus Receptus has 'and' (καί) here instead; see the note on the text.

04.r: The second man of the parable.
04.n: Abbott-Smith cites this verse under his second sense: a subordinate who collected taxes or tolls in a particular district. This study renders it 'toll collector' throughout.

05.r: He keeps his distance, inside the temple but away from the front.
05.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'from afar, afar' and cites this verse. That he stood back out of a sense of unworthiness is a reasonable reading, not stated.

06.r: He stands, as one did to pray.
06.n: A perfect participle of the verb 'stand', literally 'having stood', which the YLT keeps; in this verb the perfect describes the standing position itself.

08.r: With 'not': he would not bring himself to it.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to will, be willing, wish, desire'. An imperfect: his holding back went on as he stood.

09.r: Not even the smallest gesture of looking up.
09.n: Abbott-Smith relates this word to μηδέ as οὐ is related to μή. After 'not', it means 'not even'.

10.r: The article, used where English says 'his'.
10.n: Literally 'the eyes', as the YLT has it.

12.r: Raising the eyes toward heaven, the posture of prayer he will not take.
12.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to lift up, raise' and lists this verse among uses with 'eyes'. The Textus Receptus places the word differently in the sentence; the sense is the same.

13.r: The direction of the look he will not give.

14.r: Greek says 'the heaven'; English does not use the article.

15.r: Heaven above, where God is addressed.
15.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'the vault or firmament of heaven, the sky'. Looking up to the sky is looking toward God.

16.r: Sets what he does against what he will not do.
16.n: Abbott-Smith calls this particle stronger than δέ.

17.r: He beats his chest over and over.
17.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to strike, smite, beat', and lists this verse for mourners striking the breast. The imperfect pictures repeated blows, which the YLT's 'was smiting' keeps.

19.r: The article, with 'his', English leaves it out.

20.r: His chest, struck in grief over his sin.
20.n: Abbott-Smith names striking the breast as a sign of penitence and cites this verse.

23.r: The article, here marking the address to God.
23.n: The Greek says 'the God', in the vocative sense; the Geneva and DRC show it as 'O God'.

25.r: A plea that God's anger over his sin be turned to favour.
25.n: An aorist passive imperative: literally 'be propitiated'. Abbott-Smith gives the classical sense, with a person as object, 'to conciliate, appease', and notes that the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew סָלַח, to forgive, and כָּפַר in the piel, the verb of atonement. This study writes 'be propitious' (favourably disposed) to keep it apart from the Greek verb for mercy; the KJV's 'be merciful' gives the sense but hides the word.

27.r: The article: he calls himself 'the sinner'.
27.n: The Greek has the article, 'the sinner', which only the YLT keeps; the others say 'a sinner'. Whether it means 'the sinner that I am' or something stronger is a matter of reading.

28.r: He names himself by what he is before God.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus opens with καί, 'and', where our text has δέ, so the KJV and YLT begin 'And the publican'; it also adds εἰς before 'his breast', which is why the KJV reads 'smote upon his breast' and the YLT 'on his breast'. It places ἐπᾶραι, 'to lift up', at a different point in the sentence, which does not change the sense.
